name: Distal radius fracture
populations: snow, skate and roller sport participants
people after a fall on an outstretched hand
summary: A break of the distal radius, most often from a fall on an outstretched hand; the classic Colles pattern is dorsally displaced. Common in older women and children; needs same-day imaging and a neurovascular check.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Cast or fixation then rehabilitation; most trial outcomes are measured at 12 months

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Radiographs (PA and lateral); the Lafontaine criteria flag fractures at risk of secondary displacement

keyFacts.label: Older adults
keyFacts.value: Casting is recommended for adults over 65 because long-term outcomes are similar with surgery; trade-offs exist between pain and grip and range (WRIST analyses)

keyFacts.label: Prevention (CRPS)
keyFacts.value: Vitamin C 500 mg daily for 50 days: CRPS RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.33–0.91) in a 3-trial meta-analysis

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Children and older adults carry the greatest risk; 87% of the older-adult WRIST trial participants were women

keyFacts.label: Children
keyFacts.value: Torus (buckle) fractures: a soft bandage was equivalent to rigid immobilisation for pain at 3 days (FORCE)

overview:
A distal radius fracture is a break of the radius within a few centimetres of the wrist joint, most often after a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH). It is one of the most common fractures: children and older adults carry the greatest risk, and its prevalence has risen in both groups over about 40 years [r1]. The classic Colles pattern is a dorsally displaced and angulated metaphyseal fracture. A volar-displaced (Smith) fracture and articular-rim (Barton) fractures are less common patterns (clinical classification).

Treatment depends on age, displacement, fracture stability, the patient's activity level and preference. In older adults, a secondary analysis of the WRIST trial (adults over 60 with unstable fractures) states that casting is recommended for adults older than 65 years because similar long-term outcomes are achieved regardless of treatment [r2]. Casting gives less pain and better appearance, while surgery gave better grip strength and range of motion in another WRIST analysis [r3], and exact restoration of anatomy was not associated with better 12-month outcomes in older adults [r4]. In younger adults and those with displaced fractures that need fixation, K-wires and volar locking plates gave similar wrist function at 12 months in the DRAFFT trial [r5]. Physiotherapists lead hand, wrist and function rehabilitation, screen for complications such as acute carpal tunnel syndrome and complex regional pain syndrome, and address falls and bone health.

epidemiology.text:
Distal radius fractures are among the most common fractures. The paediatric and elderly populations are at greatest risk, and data over the past 40 years show a rising prevalence in both [r1]. The WRIST trial, which enrolled adults over 60 years with unstable distal radius fractures, had a mean age of about 71 years and 87% of participants were women [r2]. In a Singapore cohort of 572 patients aged 60 or over with a hip fracture, 29 (5%) had a distal radius fracture in the preceding 10 years, and the authors concluded that screening for osteoporosis at a distal radius fracture might benefit only a small fraction of patients [r6]. Population incidence figures by age and sex were not retrieved for this page, so none are quoted.

Instability predicts who will lose alignment in a cast. In a 167-case series, secondary displacement after satisfactory reduction correlated with the sum of five findings: dorsal tilt over 20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular radiocarpal involvement, an associated ulnar fracture and age over 60 years [r7].

intrinsic: Older age and female sex: 87% of the older-adult WRIST participants were women [r2]
Osteoporosis and low bone density (a fragility mechanism; individual risk is not quantified in the retrieved sources) [r6]
Childhood and adolescence: the paediatric peak includes torus (buckle) fractures, the most common wrist fracture in children [r1,r10]
Poor balance, slowed protective reactions and neuromuscular impairment that raise fall risk (clinical)
Fracture-specific instability markers: dorsal tilt over 20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular extension, ulnar fracture, age over 60 [r7]
extrinsic: Falls on an outstretched hand from standing height, particularly on wet, icy or uneven surfaces (clinical)
Wheeled and board sports (skating, snowboarding, skateboarding, cycling) that cause falls forward on to the hands (clinical)
Higher-energy trauma in younger adults (road accidents, falls from height) that produce comminuted or intra-articular fractures (clinical)

mechanism.summary: The classic distal radius fracture follows a fall forward on to an outstretched hand with the wrist forced into extension. The ground reaction force travels up the hand and through the carpus into the distal radius, loading the metaphysis. The volar cortex fails in tension and the fracture line runs dorsally, where compression crushes the dorsal cortex. The distal fragment is displaced and tilted dorsally with radial shortening, which gives the 'dinner-fork' deformity of the Colles pattern (clinical biomechanics).
sequence: The person trips or slips and falls forward, reaching out to protect the head and trunk.
The arm is extended and the palm strikes the ground with the wrist in marked extension (about 60–90 degrees; clinical estimate).
The ground reaction force passes through the carpus, mainly the scaphoid and lunate, into the articular surface of the distal radius.
The volar cortex fails in tension and the fracture line crosses the metaphysis within about 2–3 cm of the radiocarpal joint [r5].
Dorsal compression crushes cancellous bone, especially in osteoporotic metaphysis, so the distal fragment tilts dorsally and shortens (clinical biomechanics).
The distal fragment, with the hand, displaces dorsally and radially, and the ulnar styloid may avulse or the TFCC may be strained.
Swelling and haematoma fill the volar and dorsal soft tissues. The median nerve and carpal tunnel are close to the fracture and are at risk (see red flags).

variants.name: Smith (reverse Colles) fracture
variants.description: A fall on the back of a flexed wrist or a direct blow to the dorsum causes a volarly displaced distal fragment. It is usually less stable and often needs fixation (clinical).

variants.name: Intra-articular and Barton fractures
variants.description: Higher-energy axial load splits the joint surface. A volar or dorsal rim shear fracture of the radius (Barton) is unstable and typically needs surgery (clinical).

variants.name: Paediatric torus (buckle) and greenstick fractures
variants.description: In children the metaphysis buckles (torus) or breaks on one side (greenstick). A soft bandage was equivalent to rigid immobilisation for torus fractures [r10].

variants.name: Physeal (Salter–Harris) injuries
variants.description: In skeletally immature wrists the distal radial physis can separate. A growth plate injury needs orthopaedic review (see related: physeal fracture).

variants.name: Associated ulnar styloid and carpal injuries
variants.description: Fractures of the ulnar styloid, scaphoid or injuries to the TFCC and scapholunate ligament can accompany the fracture; look for them clinically and radiologically (clinical).

anatomy.text: The distal radius forms the proximal articular surface of the wrist, with the scaphoid and lunate fossae. Its metaphysis is thin-walled cancellous bone, which is why it fails first in a fall and why osteoporosis makes it fragile. The articular surface normally tilts slightly toward the palm and radially. In the WRIST analysis, radial inclination of 22 degrees and an ulnar variance of 0 mm were taken as the normal reference values [r4]. The ulna joins the radius at the distal radioulnar joint, and the TFCC stabilises that joint. The median nerve, flexor tendons and radial artery run on the palmar side, and the extensor tendons lie in compartments on the dorsal side.

structures.name: Distal radius metaphysis
structures.role: Thin cortical shell with cancellous core. It transfers load from the hand to the forearm and is the usual fracture site

structures.name: Radial styloid and radiocarpal articular surface
structures.role: Articulates with the scaphoid and lunate; intra-articular extension changes the prognosis and stability

structures.name: Distal radioulnar joint, TFCC and ulnar styloid
structures.role: Stabilise forearm rotation; may be injured with the fracture

structures.name: Median nerve and carpal tunnel
structures.role: Lie close to the volar surface; swelling or displacement can compress the nerve

structures.name: Wrist extensor and flexor tendons
structures.role: Dorsal tendons (especially extensor pollicis longus) can be damaged by displaced fragments or fixation hardware; flexors lie beneath the volar plate

structures.name: Distal radial physis
structures.role: In children, the growth plate is a zone of relative weakness and may be involved

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Bone fails when the load applied exceeds its capacity. In the distal radius the bending and compressive load of a fall on an outstretched hand exceeds the strength of the thin metaphyseal cortex. Osteoporotic bone has a lower failure load, so low-energy falls can break it (fragility fracture; standard bone biology). The fracture disrupts the cortex and trabeculae, tears the periosteum and marrow vessels, and creates a haematoma. The pattern of failure (extra-articular, partial or complete articular) determines stability and, with age, the risk of secondary displacement [r7].

Healing follows the usual sequence of fracture haematoma, inflammation, soft callus, hard callus and remodelling (see the micro animation). In older adults, anatomic restoration was not clearly associated with better 12-month patient-reported outcomes, which is why treatment is individualised [r4].

structures.name: Distal radius metaphysis
structures.effect: Extra-articular or intra-articular fracture with dorsal tilt, shortening and radial deviation of the distal fragment (Colles pattern)

structures.name: Ulnar styloid and distal radioulnar joint
structures.effect: Avulsion fracture of the ulnar styloid or TFCC and DRUJ injury may accompany the fracture

structures.name: Median nerve
structures.effect: Acute compression from swelling, haematoma or displaced bone. Median nerve compression was reported in 18.5% (12 of 65) of the volar plate group in the WRIST complications analysis [r8]

structures.name: Wrist ligaments and scaphoid
structures.effect: Scapholunate ligament injury and scaphoid fracture can accompany the injury (clinical)

structures.name: Soft tissues and tendons
structures.effect: Swelling, bruising and later adhesions limit finger and wrist motion; extensor tendon injury is a recognised late problem (clinical)

muscles.name: Forearm flexors and extensors
muscles.effect: Immobilisation causes disuse weakness and stiffness. Grip strength and range of motion differed by treatment, and surgery maximised both in one analysis [r3].

muscles.name: Finger and thumb intrinsic muscles
muscles.effect: Swelling and a long period without finger motion lead to stiffness and weakness; early finger movement is a core rehabilitation target (clinical; the Cochrane evidence for specific interventions is very low quality [r12]).

muscles.name: Shoulder and elbow muscles
muscles.effect: Sling use and guarding can lead to shoulder stiffness, particularly in older adults (clinical).

cellular.description: Bleeding fills the fracture gap. Inflammatory cells clear debris and release growth factors that recruit osteoprogenitor cells (standard fracture biology).
Chondrocytes and fibroblasts form a cartilage-rich callus that bridges the gap and gives early stability (standard fracture biology).
The callus mineralises to woven bone. Union is slower in osteoporotic bone (standard fracture biology).
Woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone and the cortex remodels along lines of load (standard fracture biology).

systems.effect: In older adults a distal radius fracture can signal low bone density. In one cohort 5% of hip-fracture patients had a preceding distal radius fracture, and the authors questioned routine osteoporosis screening on this basis [r6]. Local policy for bone-health assessment applies.
Nerve compression (median nerve) can occur acutely [r8]. Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) can follow wrist fracture; vitamin C reduced CRPS risk in a meta-analysis (see management) [r11].
Haematoma and oedema raise soft-tissue pressure; tight casts or severe swelling can compromise perfusion (red flags).
Immobilisation affects the elbow, shoulder and hand, so early mobilisation of all uninjured joints is important [r12].
Fear of falling, loss of independence and fear of loading the wrist can limit recovery, particularly in older adults (clinical).

grading.system: Descriptive classification (clinical convention) and AO/OTA groups

grades.description: Extra-articular metaphyseal fracture with dorsal angulation, dorsal displacement and radial shortening after a fall on an extended wrist.
grades.prognosis: Stability depends on comminution, dorsal tilt and age [r7]

grades.description: Volarly displaced distal fragment, usually from a fall on a flexed wrist or a blow to the dorsum.
grades.prognosis: Often unstable; surgical fixation is commonly needed (clinical)

grades.grade: Barton and intra-articular fractures (AO/OTA B and C)
grades.description: Rim shear or complete articular disruption from higher-energy axial load.
grades.prognosis: Operative fixation to restore the joint surface is common (clinical)

grades.grade: Paediatric torus, greenstick and physeal fractures
grades.description: Buckle of the cortex, a one-sided break, or a growth plate injury.
grades.prognosis: Torus fractures recover well with a soft bandage and discharge [r10]; physeal injuries need orthopaedic review

timeframes.summary: Bone union usually takes about 6–12 weeks in adults (typical), while recovery of grip and range of motion continues to about 12 months, the usual follow-up point in trials [r3,r5]. Immobilisation lasts about 4–6 weeks in most adults (a common clinical convention) and is shorter in children with torus fractures [r10].

healing.description: Fracture haematoma, pain, swelling and bruising; reduce and immobilise
Cartilaginous bridging; cast or fixation protects alignment (4–6 weeks typical)
Mineralised bridging callus; clinical and radiographic union; progressive loading
Bone remodels; grip, range and function continue to improve through 12 months [r3]

milestones.label: Fingers, elbow and shoulder moving
milestones.note: Begin on day 1; there is no need to wait for the cast to come off (clinical convention)

milestones.label: Cast removal or transition to a removable splint
milestones.note: Typical clinical timing; follow the surgeon and radiographic review

milestones.label: Wrist and forearm range of motion regained
milestones.note: Most functional range returns in the weeks after immobilisation (typical)

milestones.label: Weight-bearing through the hand (e.g. press-up)
milestones.note: Once union is confirmed and pain allows (clinical convention)

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, usually about 3–4 months for impact or fall-risk activity and longer for heavy manual work (a common clinical convention). Return requires radiographic union, near-full range, grip within about 80–90% of the other side and confident, pain-free loading. Protective equipment (wrist guards in board sports) is advisable.

symptoms: Immediate wrist pain after a fall on an outstretched hand
Swelling and bruising around the wrist and distal forearm
Visible wrist deformity in displaced fractures (dinner-fork deformity in Colles pattern)
Inability to grip, load or rotate the forearm because of pain
Numbness or tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers (median nerve)
signs: Tenderness over the distal radius and sometimes the ulnar styloid
Swelling and ecchymosis of the wrist and dorsum of the hand
Deformity with dorsal prominence of the distal fragment and a hollow volarly (Colles)
Reduced and painful wrist and forearm movement
Altered sensation or capillary refill that needs urgent attention

subjective: Mechanism: fall on an outstretched hand, height of fall, or higher-energy trauma
Hand dominance, occupation, hobbies and the function the patient needs to return to
Previous fractures, falls, osteoporosis and medications that affect bone or healing
Numbness, tingling, increasing pain or tight swelling (neurovascular status)
Pre-injury function, living situation and support, particularly in older adults
Anticoagulants and other factors that affect surgical or casting plans
observation: Wrist deformity and skin integrity (open wound or tenting)
Swelling, bruising and colour of the hand and fingers
Finger posture and ability to flex and extend them
palpation: Distal radius and ulnar styloid tenderness
Anatomical snuffbox and scaphoid tubercle (to screen for associated scaphoid fracture)
Elbow and forearm tenderness (proximal radius or ulna injury)
rangeOfMotion: Finger, thumb, elbow and shoulder movement (mobilise uninjured joints)
Wrist and forearm range only when the fracture and its protection allow
Compare with the opposite side after union
strength: Grip dynamometry compared with the other side after immobilisation
Shoulder and scapular strength in older adults who used a sling
neuro: Median nerve: thumb, index and middle finger sensation and thumb opposition
Ulnar and radial nerve sensation and motor function
Capillary refill, radial pulse and finger perfusion
Repeat neurovascular checks, especially after casting or surgery
functional: PRWE or QuickDASH items on daily tasks
Observed use of the hand for dressing, eating and toileting
Fall-risk screen: balance, gait and footwear

specialTests.name: Radiographic assessment of reduction and alignment (PA and lateral views)
specialTests.purpose: Describe displacement, comminution, joint involvement and instability
specialTests.procedure: Review the PA and lateral radiographs for dorsal tilt, radial inclination, ulnar variance, articular step or gap, and ulnar styloid or DRUJ injury.
specialTests.positive: Displacement or angulation beyond local thresholds. In the WRIST analysis, 22 degrees of radial inclination and 0 mm of ulnar variance served as normal references [r4].

specialTests.name: Lafontaine instability criteria
specialTests.purpose: Estimate the risk of secondary displacement in a cast
specialTests.procedure: Count the findings on the first radiograph: dorsal tilt over 20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular involvement, associated ulnar fracture, and age over 60 years.
specialTests.positive: Secondary displacement risk rises with the number of findings present [r7].

specialTests.name: Snuffbox and scaphoid tubercle palpation
specialTests.purpose: Screen for an associated or missed scaphoid fracture
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the anatomical snuffbox and the scaphoid tubercle, and apply axial thumb compression.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness suggests a scaphoid injury; arrange scaphoid-specific imaging if radiographs are normal.

specialTests.name: Neurovascular examination
specialTests.purpose: Detect acute carpal tunnel syndrome, compartment syndrome or vascular injury
specialTests.procedure: Test median, ulnar and radial sensation and motor function, finger perfusion and pain on passive finger stretch, and repeat after each treatment step.
specialTests.positive: New numbness, increasing pain, pallor or pain on passive finger stretch: escalate urgently (median nerve compression occurred in 18.5% of one plated group [r8]).

clinicalRules.name: Lafontaine criteria for instability
clinicalRules.description: Dorsal tilt over 20 degrees, dorsal comminution, intra-articular radiocarpal involvement, an associated ulnar fracture, and age over 60 years were associated with secondary displacement after initial reduction in a 167-case series [r7].

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the DRAFFT trial (score out of 100) [r5]

outcomeMeasures.name: Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire (MHQ)
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the WRIST trial analyses [r2,r3]

outcomeMeasures.name: Grip strength and wrist and forearm range of motion
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective recovery measures; surgery maximised grip and range in one analysis [r3]

imaging.findings: Fracture line, displacement, dorsal tilt, shortening, intra-articular extension, ulnar styloid fracture

imaging.indication: Intra-articular fractures or when joint surface congruity is unclear before surgery
imaging.findings: Articular step or gap, comminution and fragment position

imaging.modality: MRI or CT for suspected occult carpal injury
imaging.indication: Persistent snuffbox tenderness or pain with normal radiographs
imaging.findings: Occult scaphoid or other carpal fracture, ligament injury

differentials.name: Scaphoid fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Snuffbox tenderness and pain with axial thumb compression; may coexist with a distal radius fracture and be missed on initial radiographs.

differentials.name: TFCC injury
differentials.distinguishing: Ulnar-sided wrist pain and clicking with rotation; the fovea and ulnar styloid are tender, and radiographs of the radius may be normal.

differentials.name: Scapholunate ligament injury
differentials.distinguishing: Dorsal wrist pain after extension injury with a positive scaphoid shift test and widened scapholunate interval on radiographs.

differentials.name: Paediatric physeal fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Distal radial physeal tenderness in a child; a Salter–Harris pattern on radiographs.

differentials.name: Wrist sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain without bony tenderness and normal radiographs. Diagnosis only after fracture is excluded.

differentials.name: Distal radioulnar joint injury or Galeazzi pattern
differentials.distinguishing: Forearm fracture with distal radioulnar joint instability; tenderness over the ulnar head and pain on forearm rotation.

differentials.name: Carpal dislocation (lunate or perilunate)
differentials.distinguishing: High-energy mechanism, severe swelling and pain, median nerve symptoms and a characteristic carpal alignment change on the lateral radiograph.

redFlags: Increasing numbness or pain in the median distribution after the injury, a cast or surgery: suspect acute carpal tunnel syndrome. Release a tight cast or dressing, elevate, and arrange same-day emergency review (median nerve compression was reported in 18.5% of one plated group [r8]).
Severe pain out of proportion, pain on passive finger stretch, tense forearm swelling or pallor: suspect compartment syndrome or vascular compromise. Refer to emergency immediately.
Open wound, skin tenting, gross deformity, or loss of finger perfusion: suspect an open or irreducible fracture. Refer to emergency immediately.
Snuffbox tenderness or pain with normal radiographs: suspect a scaphoid fracture. Immobilise and arrange further imaging or review.
Disproportionate burning pain, swelling, colour or temperature change, allodynia and stiffness out of keeping with the injury: suspect complex regional pain syndrome. Refer early.
Sudden inability to extend the thumb after fracture or fixation: suspect extensor pollicis longus rupture. Refer to a hand surgeon.
Low-trauma fracture in an older adult with no prior bone health assessment: arrange a medical review for bone health and falls risk.

management.principles: Treatment is individualised using age, activity level, fracture pattern and stability, and the patient's preferences. An AAOS clinical practice guideline exists and cites 35 randomised trials, although adverse events are incompletely reported in them [r9]; its individual recommendations were not retrievable for this page, so the treatment labels below rest on the trials and reviews cited. In adults over 60 years with unstable fractures, casting and surgery gave similar long-term outcomes, with trade-offs between pain and appearance (better with casting) and grip strength and range of motion (better with surgery) [r2,r3]. In the WRIST trial the casting group chose not to have surgery and was not randomised, so comparisons with it are non-randomised [r8]. In children, soft-bandage treatment of torus fractures was equivalent to rigid immobilisation for pain at 3 days [r10]. Whatever the treatment, early finger, elbow and shoulder movement, oedema control and screening for complications are essential [r12].

medical.name: Closed reduction and cast immobilisation
medical.description: Reduction under local or regional anaesthetic where displaced, then a cast or splint for about 4–6 weeks (clinical convention). The WRIST analysis states that casting is recommended for adults over 65 because long-term outcomes are similar to surgery [r2]; the evidence label here is limited because the casting group was not randomised. Use it for low-demand older adults with stable or acceptable alignment. Casting gave less pain and better appearance than surgery, whereas surgery gave more grip strength and range of motion [r3]. The WRIST casting group was non-randomised [r8].

medical.name: Surgical fixation (K-wires, volar locking plate, external fixator)
medical.description: Considered for unstable, displaced, intra-articular or high-demand cases. In DRAFFT (461 adults with dorsally displaced fractures needing fixation) K-wires and volar locking plates gave no clinically relevant difference in PRWE at 12 months [r5]. Complications differ: median nerve compression was reported in 18.5% of plated cases and pin-site infection in 23.2% of pinned cases in the WRIST analysis [r8].

medical.name: Vitamin C after fracture (CRPS prevention)
medical.description: A meta-analysis of 3 placebo-controlled trials (875 patients) found that 500 mg of vitamin C daily for 50 days from the day of injury reduced CRPS-I risk (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.33–0.91); heterogeneity was 65% [r11].

medical.name: Soft bandage for paediatric torus fractures
medical.description: In 965 children aged 4–15 years, offer of a soft bandage with immediate discharge was equivalent to rigid immobilisation for pain at 3 days (adjusted difference −0.10, 95% CI −0.37 to 0.17), with no difference in function over 6 weeks [r10].

medical.name: Analgesia and elevation
medical.description: Simple analgesia, elevation above heart level and early finger movement to control pain and oedema (clinical convention).

medical.name: Bone health and falls assessment
medical.description: Review for osteoporosis and falls risk in older adults with a low-trauma fracture. The value of routine screening after an isolated distal radius fracture is debated, since only 5% of one hip-fracture cohort had one in the prior decade [r6].

physio.name: Early mobilisation of fingers, thumb, elbow and shoulder with oedema control
physio.description: Start on day 1 during immobilisation: full finger flexion and extension, thumb opposition, forearm elevation, elbow and shoulder range. Cochrane evidence on specific hand-therapy interventions during immobilisation is of very low quality, but the approach is low risk [r12].

physio.name: Structured home exercise program with initial instruction
physio.description: After immobilisation, a supervised initial session with a written progressive home program. After volar plate fixation, two small trials gave low-quality evidence in favour of a structured home exercise program preceded by instruction or coaching over physiotherapy or occupational therapy [r12].

physio.name: Supervised physiotherapy or occupational therapy
physio.description: Routine therapy in addition to home exercise instructions made no clinically important difference in four heterogeneous trials (low-quality evidence). Reserve for people who cannot self-manage, have complications, or have high-demand goals [r12].

physio.name: Strengthening and graded loading
physio.description: Progressive grip, wrist and forearm loading and weight-bearing after union. No specific protocol is supported by high-quality evidence; progress by clinical criteria [r12].

physio.name: Falls prevention and balance training
physio.description: Balance, strength and gait training in older adults at risk of falls, addressing home hazards and footwear (clinical).

physio.name: Passive modalities (ultrasound, ice, whirlpool, passive mobilisation, pulsed electromagnetic field)
physio.description: Single-intervention trials showed no clinically significant differences compared with no intervention in very low quality evidence; some showed short-term benefit in single small trials. Do not prioritise over exercise [r12].

education: Most wrist fractures heal well, but recovery of grip and range of motion continues for up to a year.
Move your fingers, elbow and shoulder every day, and keep the hand elevated while swelling settles.
Seek urgent help if numbness, tingling, severe pain or colour change develop in the hand, especially under a cast.
Casting and surgery often give similar long-term results in older adults, so the choice depends on your priorities for pain, strength and movement.
A fall that breaks a wrist is a reason to review bone health and falls risk with your doctor.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is staged by fracture healing and fixation stability: mobilise uninjured joints and control oedema during immobilisation, restore wrist and forearm range once allowed, rebuild grip and wrist strength, and return to load and function with falls prevention. The Cochrane evidence for specific rehabilitation interventions is of low or very low quality and insufficient to define the best program [r12], so dosages below are common clinical conventions. Always confirm the surgeon's or doctor's restrictions, particularly after fixation.

stages.name: Protect & mobilise adjacent joints
goals: Full finger, thumb, elbow and shoulder movement
precautions: Do not remove cast or splint unless instructed
Check for numbness, colour change, increasing pain and pin-site problems
Report signs of acute carpal tunnel syndrome or CRPS immediately

exercises.name: Finger and thumb flexion, extension and opposition
exercises.cues: Make a full fist, then open fully; touch each fingertip with the thumb

exercises.name: Elevation and gentle oedema pumping
exercises.dosage: Hand above the heart, with 20 finger pumps, 3–4 times daily
exercises.cues: Elbow supported, hand higher than elbow

exercises.name: Shoulder flexion and elevation range
exercises.cues: Lift the arm overhead without gripping the cast

exercises.name: Elbow flexion and extension
exercises.cues: Full range; avoid forearm rotation if restricted

exercises.name: Contralateral grip training (cross-education)
exercises.cues: Controlled effort; keep the injured arm relaxed

progressionCriteria: Oedema controlled and fingers fully mobile
No signs of neurovascular compromise or CRPS
Surgeon or doctor cleared cast or splint removal

stages.name: Restore wrist & forearm range
precautions: No forceful loading or weight-bearing through the wrist yet
After fixation, follow the surgeon's range and weight limits
Avoid heavy passive stretching into pain (CRPS risk)

exercises.name: Active wrist flexion and extension
exercises.cues: Forearm supported on a table; move to comfortable end range

exercises.name: Active forearm pronation and supination
exercises.cues: Elbow tucked to the side, slow and controlled

exercises.name: Radial and ulnar deviation
exercises.cues: Keep the forearm still and move only the wrist

exercises.name: Wrist flexor and extensor stretches
exercises.cues: Gentle, pain-free stretch; no overpressure

exercises.name: Tendon gliding series
exercises.cues: Straight, hook, full fist, table-top, straight fist

progressionCriteria: At least 75% of the other wrist range in flexion and extension
Pain at 3/10 or less with daily use
Radiographic or clinical union confirmed by the treating doctor

stages.name: Strength & graded loading
precautions: Begin weight-bearing only after union is confirmed
Progress load if there is no increase in pain or swelling in the next 24 hours
Treat persistent swelling, stiffness or burning pain as a possible CRPS sign and refer

exercises.name: Wrist extension with dumbbell
exercises.cues: Forearm supported; slow lowering

exercises.name: Wrist flexion with dumbbell
exercises.cues: Control the movement through full range

exercises.name: Grip strengthening (putty, gripper or towel wring)
exercises.cues: Squeeze firmly with the wrist in neutral

exercises.name: Hammer or weighted-bar forearm rotation
exercises.cues: Slow and controlled; keep the elbow at the side

exercises.name: Wall or incline push-up
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12, progressing to the floor as tolerated
exercises.cues: Wrists under shoulders, even weight through both hands

progressionCriteria: Grip strength at least 80% of the other side
Tolerates body-weight loading through the wrist with minimal pain
Wrist range within about 10% of the other side
Completes usual daily tasks without a flare

stages.name: Function, power & falls prevention
goals: Return to full work, sport and hobbies
Restore speed and impact tolerance if needed
precautions: Use wrist guards for board sports and high fall-risk activity
Continue to monitor for late complications such as tendon problems or persistent stiffness

exercises.name: Farmer carry (grip endurance)
exercises.cues: Tall posture and neutral wrists

exercises.name: Heavy grip and wrist strength maintenance
exercises.cues: Symptom-guided progression

exercises.name: Task-specific practice (tools, keyboard, sport skills)
exercises.cues: Keep the wrist near neutral and take breaks

exercises.name: Single-leg balance and gait training (falls prevention)
exercises.cues: Soft knee and quiet trunk; progress surface and task difficulty

exercises.name: Safe-fall and protective-reaction practice for sport
exercises.cues: Roll and absorb the force through the whole body rather than an outstretched hand

progressionCriteria: Grip strength at least 90% of the other side
Pain-free through full range and loading
Bone health and falls plan in place for older adults

criteria: Radiographic and clinical union confirmed by the treating doctor
Wrist and forearm range of motion within about 10% of the other side
Grip strength at least 80–90% of the other side (a common clinical convention)
Pain-free with sport-specific loading and weight-bearing through the wrist
Confident protective reactions and use of wrist guards where indicated
No signs of CRPS, nerve symptoms or tendon problems
tests: Grip and pinch dynamometry compared with the other hand

prognosis: Most distal radius fractures heal, but function recovers over months and trials follow patients to 12 months [r3,r5]. In adults over 60, casting and surgery give similar long-term outcomes [r2], and exact anatomic restoration was not associated with better 12-month outcomes [r4]. Complications differ by treatment: in the WRIST analysis, the casting group had a higher rate of any-severity complications than the internal fixation group (adjusted rate ratio 1.88, 95% CI 1.22–2.88), median nerve compression affected 18.5% of the plated group, and pin-site infection affected 23.2% of the pinned group [r8]. In DRAFFT, K-wire and plate fixation had no difference in wrist function or complications at 12 months [r5]. CRPS can follow wrist fracture, and vitamin C reduced its risk in a meta-analysis [r11]. Children with torus fractures recover equally well with a soft bandage [r10].
prevention: Address falls risk in older adults: balance, strength and gait training, home hazard review, vision, medication and footwear review (clinical).
Review bone health after a low-trauma fracture, noting that screening policy after an isolated distal radius fracture varies [r6].
Use wrist guards and sensible protective equipment for skating, snowboarding and similar sports (clinical).
Teach safe falling techniques (rolling, absorbing force through the body) for sport participants (clinical).
clinicalPearls: Always check the median nerve and finger perfusion before and after any cast, splint or surgery, and repeat the check at each visit [r8].
In people over about 60, an excellent X-ray does not guarantee a better outcome: patient preferences, activity and priorities for pain versus grip should shape the decision [r3,r4].
Start finger, elbow and shoulder movement on day 1; stiffness in uninjured joints is a preventable cause of poor function [r12].
Counting Lafontaine findings on the first radiograph helps predict which fractures will slip in a cast [r7].
Disproportionate, burning pain with swelling and colour or temperature change in the weeks after fracture should be treated as CRPS until proved otherwise; refer early (clinical).
Always ask about snuffbox tenderness: a scaphoid fracture can coexist with, or be mistaken for, a distal radius fracture.

animation.title: How a distal radius (Colles) fracture happens

forces.label: Ground force through the outstretched hand

captions.text: An older woman with osteoporosis steps off a kerb and loses her balance.
She falls forward and reaches out to protect herself.
The palm strikes the ground and the wrist is forced into extension.
The ground force passes up the hand and loads the distal radius.
The wrist is painful, swollen and deformed.
Zooming into the right wrist, viewed from the palm side.

actions.text: Displaced extra-articular fracture ~2 cm from the joint
Median nerve at risk: watch for acute carpal tunnel syndrome

captions.text: The distal radius has a thin cortical shell around cancellous bone, weaker still in osteoporosis.
A fall on an outstretched hand drives load up through the carpus into the radius.
The metaphysis fails and the distal fragment displaces dorsally and shortens.
The ulnar styloid often fractures or avulses at the same time.
Haematoma and swelling can compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
Reduction and a cast, or fixation, restore and protect alignment.
Healthy trabecular bone, thinner and less dense in osteoporosis.
The bone fails under the compressive and bending load.
A fracture haematoma forms around the broken ends.
Inflammatory cells clear debris and release growth factors.
A soft callus bridges the gap and gives early stability.
The callus mineralises to woven bone as union is established.
Remodelling restores lamellar bone while grip and range continue to improve.
